subject: ent
title: Vocal cord paralysis

steps.tx: The **recurrent laryngeal nerve** supplies all the intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid, which receives the **external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve**. The right nerve loops around the subclavian artery while the left nerve dips into the chest and loops around the **aortic arch**, so left palsy is commoner in lung and mediastinal disease. High vagal lesions add palatal weakness, while superior laryngeal injury after thyroid surgery robs singers of pitch range and projection.
steps.say: Both vocal cords move because the recurrent laryngeal nerves supply nearly every small laryngeal muscle except one. The right nerve takes a short loop in the neck, but the left nerve travels deep into the chest and curves around the aorta. That long chest journey exposes the left nerve to lung tumours, enlarged nodes and aortic disease, so left sided palsy appears more often in clinics. Injury to the superior laryngeal nerve during thyroid surgery involves the cricothyroid muscle and removes the upper pitch range that singers need.

steps.tx: Palsy follows damage at any point along the **vagus nerve** pathway, from jugular foramen syndromes at the skull base to neck surgery on the thyroid, carotid or cervical spine. Chest disease striking the left nerve includes apical lung cancer, oesophageal cancer and **aortic aneurysm**, while an enlarged left atrium can compress the nerve in **Ortner syndrome**. Intubation trauma may dislocate the arytenoid and mimic palsy, and unexplained cases need contrast imaging from the skull base to the aortopulmonary window.
steps.say: Many different diseases can silence a vocal cord because the nerve travels all the way from the brainstem to the chest. Surgeons meet palsies after thyroid, carotid and neck spine operations, while physicians blame lung cancers, food pipe tumours and bulging aortic aneurysms. A dilated left atrium in severe mitral valve disease can squeeze the left nerve and cause the hoarseness called Ortner syndrome. When no cause is obvious, doctors order a contrast scan that traces the whole nerve from the skull base to the chest. A dislocated arytenoid after intubation can look exactly like a palsy but needs mechanical correction.

steps.tx: Flexible **laryngoscopy** reveals the still cord resting near the midline, often with bowing, pooled secretions and thin fluid aspiration, while **stroboscopy** grades vibration for voice professionals. The voice turns breathy and double toned, tires quickly, and pairs with a weak bovine cough. **Speech therapy** comes first, with temporary injection medialisation protecting swallowers and professional voices early, and permanent thyroplasty or arytenoid adduction reserved until after nine to twelve months without recovery.
steps.say: The scope usually shows one cord parked near the midline with a bowed edge, while secretions collect above the voice box and thin liquids slip into the airway. Patients speak with a breathy and rough double tone that fades with use, and their cough sounds weak and bovine. Speech therapy starts first and rebuilds closure and safe swallowing, while a temporary gel injection pushes the weak cord toward the midline. Surgeons wait about nine to twelve months before offering permanent medialisation, because some injured nerves still recover.

steps.tx: The scope view shows a bowed **paramedian cord** that cannot meet its mobile partner, with pooled secretions and thin fluid **aspiration** across the glottis. This matches the examination step where **laryngoscopy** reveals bowing, pooling, and aspiration with a breathy double toned voice. In the exam, link pooling with swallowing danger, protect the airway first, and start **speech therapy** before any permanent framework surgery.
steps.say: This scope view presents one bowed cord resting near the midline beside its normal mobile partner. Secretions remain beside the still cord while thin fluids pass across the glottis into the airway. The picture explains the breathy double toned voice with a weak cough. Pooling indicates swallowing danger, so the airway needs protection first. Speech therapy remains the first step, with permanent framework surgery reserved for long standing cases.

steps.tx: **Bilateral palsy** is an airway emergency in slow motion: both cords rest near the midline because the sole opener muscle has failed, so stridor dominates while the voice stays surprisingly clear. Common triggers include thyroid surgery, advanced malignancy and neurological disease. Severe obstruction needs prompt **tracheostomy**, with later **cordotomy** or arytenoidectomy widening the airway at the price of voice quality. Never sedate or scope these patients casually without a ready airway plan.
steps.say: When both nerves fail, both cords sink toward the midline and leave only a slit for breathing. These patients often speak quite clearly, which can mislead juniors, but every breath whistles with inspiratory stridor. Thyroid surgery, spreading cancers and nerve diseases cause most bilateral palsies seen in Indian hospitals. Tight obstruction needs an urgent tracheostomy for safety, and later surgeons can widen the airway with laser cordotomy at the cost of a huskier voice. Such patients require full airway backup before any sedation or scopy.
